title: Whole-Organism Cloning vs Gene Cloning: How Dolly Was Made and How Well Cloning Works
subtitle: Dolly the sheep and a flask of bacteria copying one gene are both called cloning. So what does each kind of cloning copy, how is the copy made, and how well does each do the job it's meant for?
subject: Biology
lessonIntent: defining a clone as a genetically identical copy and separating whole-organism cloning (a new individual with the same nuclear DNA as an existing one) from gene cloning (many copies of one selected piece of DNA); tracing somatic cell nuclear transfer with Dolly (a body cell from a white-faced ewe's udder; an egg from a black-faced ewe with its nucleus removed; an electric pulse fuses them and starts division; the embryo carried by a black-faced surrogate); explaining that the clone's nuclear DNA matches the nucleus donor while its mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg, and that development and environment can still make it differ; assessing whole-organism cloning by reliability (277 fused cells, 29 embryos, one lamb, because the egg often resets the body-cell nucleus's gene switches only partly), identity and health (pregnancy losses and abnormal births are common; Dolly's illnesses do not show early ageing; later clones from her cells aged healthily), with a verdict by purpose (too unreliable for routine breeding; worth it to copy one rare or valuable animal, as with the black-footed ferret); tracing gene cloning (a gene in a plasmid vector, taken up by a bacterial host, copied at every division into billions of copies; PCR copies a gene without cells) and assessing it (very effective for a narrow, checkable aim: one bacterium is enough; colonies must be checked for the gene; rare copying errors); distinguishing the two by what exists at the end; applying this to an unseen assess item and an unseen distinguish item.

voiceover.text: In July 1996, a white-faced lamb was born in Scotland to a black-faced ewe. She was Dolly, and she wasn't that ewe's daughter. She was a clone of a different sheep. Meanwhile, labs were routinely cloning genes, copying one piece of DNA billions of times inside bacteria. So what does each kind of cloning copy, how is the copy made, and how well does each do the job it's meant for?

A clone is a genetically identical copy. The question is, a copy of what? You've met natural clones already: a banana plant grown from a piece of its parent has the same alleles as that parent. Whole-organism cloning aims to make a new individual with the same DNA as an existing one. Gene cloning makes many copies of just one selected piece of DNA. So always ask what is being copied: a whole individual, or one gene.

Here's how Dolly was made, by a method called somatic cell nuclear transfer. Somatic just means a body cell, not an egg or a sperm. Scientists took cells grown from the udder of a white-faced ewe. Then they took an egg from a black-faced ewe, and sucked out its nucleus, so the egg had no chromosomes of its own. An electric pulse fused the udder cell with the empty egg and started it dividing. After about a week, the young embryo was placed in the uterus of another black-faced ewe, who carried it to birth.

So Dolly had three mothers. Which one does she match? Her nucleus came from the white-faced ewe, so her chromosomes, and her white face, match the nucleus donor, not the egg donor or the ewe who gave birth. But she wasn't a perfect copy. Her mitochondria, which carry a little DNA of their own, came from the egg. And a clone develops in a different uterus and grows up in its own environment, so it can differ in size, markings or health.

Now assess it, starting with reliability. The team at the Roslin Institute fused 277 udder cells with eggs. Only 29 grew into embryos healthy enough to transfer, and just one became a live lamb. Why so few? As an udder cell specialised, chemical tags, like the ones on histones, switched many of its genes off. To start a whole new animal, the egg has to reset those switches, and it often does that only partly. So many clones die before or soon after birth, and some are born unusually large. Rates have improved, but most attempts still fail.

What about Dolly's health? She developed arthritis, and at six she was put down because of a lung disease caused by a virus that also infected other sheep in her flock. That alone can't show cloning aged her early. And four later clones from the same udder cells were healthy for their age at seven to nine. So effectiveness depends on the purpose. Cloning is too unreliable for everyday breeding, but it can be worth it to copy one rare animal. Cells from a black-footed ferret, frozen in 1988, have given clones, and in 2024 one of them had babies, passing on alleles previously absent from the breeding population.

Gene cloning has a narrower aim: lots of copies of one gene. Scientists put the gene into a plasmid, a small ring of DNA that bacteria carry. Here the plasmid is a vector, a carrier that moves DNA into a cell. The bacterium that takes it up is the host. Each time the host divides, it copies the plasmid as well as its own DNA, so the new cells get the gene. Bacteria can divide every half hour or so, so by the next day one cell becomes billions. There's also a way to copy a gene with no cells, called PCR. Heat separates the DNA's two strands, then, as it cools, an enzyme copies each one, so every cycle doubles the gene.

So how effective is it? Very, for its purpose. Only a few bacteria take up a plasmid, but you need just one, because it multiplies. The result is easy to check, because scientists can read the copied gene's sequence. The copies let scientists study a gene, make its protein, or put it into another organism. Its limits are small: the gene doesn't always end up in the plasmid, so colonies must be checked.

To tell them apart, ask what exists at the end that didn't before. A new organism means whole-organism cloning. Many copies of one gene means gene cloning. Two things to hold on to. The clone matches the nucleus donor. And gene cloning copies a gene; organism cloning copies an individual.

Two exam questions now. First. A company made 100 embryos by nuclear transfer, using skin cells from a prize dairy bull. Six calves were born, and four were alive at one year. Their black and white patches differed from the bull's, and from each other's. Assess the effectiveness of cloning for copying this bull. Pause here to answer.

Reliability is low: four live calves from a hundred embryos, and two of the six born died. Their nuclear DNA matches the bull's, but patches differ, because patch patterns form during development, not from genes alone. So it's worth it only for a very valuable bull. Saying different patches prove the DNA wasn't copied is the classic mistake.

Second. A zoo stores frozen skin cells from a northern white rhino that has died. Project A will make many copies of one of the rhino's genes, to study its sequence. Project B aims to produce a living rhino calf from the cells. Distinguish between the cloning used in the two projects. Pause here to answer.

Project A is gene cloning. The gene goes into a plasmid, and dividing bacteria copy it, so the product is many copies of one gene. Project B is whole-organism cloning. A skin cell's nucleus goes into an egg with its own nucleus removed, so the product is a calf whose nuclear DNA matches the rhino's. Saying both projects make a copy of the rhino is the classic mistake.

So when a question says cloning, first ask what is being copied: a whole individual, or one gene. Then trace how the copy is made, and judge it against its purpose: how reliable it is, how identical the copies are, and how healthy or useful they are.
